opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what grabbed me early on wasn't the idea of a better chatbot. It was the realization that these models had absorbed an enormous amount of human behavior. They'd read how people talk, argue, make plans, and gossip. So the question I kept coming back to was: if the model encodes something about how humans act, can we use it to simulate people, not just answer questions?

My background is in human-computer interaction, and HCI has always had a problem with social systems. When you design a social platform or a community space, you can't really prototype it. You have to launch it, get real people in, and only then see what emerges: the norms, the conflicts, the failure modes. That's expensive, and sometimes it's harmful. So I got excited about whether a foundation model could let us populate a system with believable stand-ins and watch how things unfold before any real person is affected.

The surprising part was that a single prompt could already give you a plausible-sounding person. Ask the model to respond as a college student who loves jazz, and it would. But that was a moment, not a life. The person had no memory, no continuity, no ability to plan their day or form a relationship with someone they met yesterday. What interested me most was that gap: the model had the raw material for believable behavior, and the open problem was the architecture around it. You need memory, reflection, and planning so an agent can stay coherent over time and interact with other agents in ways that produce emergent social behavior.

That's where I saw the real possibility. Foundation models gave us a new kind of material, and the interesting work was figuring out what you could build with it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says early models had absorbed enormous amounts of human behavior and that he was interested in using them to simulate people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What really caught my attention, back around the GPT-3 era, was that for the first time we had a model that seemed to carry a kind of latent knowledge about how people behave. Not just language in the narrow sense, but all these patterns of how a person responds when they're greeted, how they argue, how they plan their day, how they react to good or bad news. That knowledge had been baked in from training on an enormous amount of human-generated text.

And I come from an HCI background, so my instinct wasn't to ask "how do we get this model to answer questions correctly." It was to ask "what new kinds of interactions become possible now?" The thing I kept coming back to was this idea that we might be able to build computational agents that behave in believable, human-like ways. Not necessarily agents that are smart in some abstract sense, but agents that are socially plausible. That had been a dream in HCI and in the games community for decades. Think about The Sims, or early chatbots, or all the work on believable characters. People had tried to hand-author those behaviors with rules and scripts, and it always felt brittle, because human behavior is so open-ended.

So when I saw these models, what interested me most was that the authoring bottleneck might just dissolve. Instead of writing rules for every situation, you could describe who someone is, give them a memory of what they've experienced, and let the model fill in the behavior. That opened up questions I found really exciting: could you have an agent that wakes up, makes breakfast, goes to work, remembers a conversation it had yesterday, and lets that shape what it does tomorrow? Could a bunch of these agents interact and produce emergent social dynamics that nobody scripted?

And then there's the second layer, which is why that would matter beyond being a cool demo. If you can simulate believable human behavior, you get a new tool for prototyping social systems, for testing how a design or a policy might play out before you deploy it to real people. That combination of interaction design possibilities and a potential new scientific instrument was what pulled me in.

r001.rationale: He says early models carried latent knowledge of how people behave, learned from human-generated text, and that this capacity most interested him.

astra-6.text:
What interested me most was the possibility of using language to create richer models of human behavior. In human-computer interaction, we often think about a person interacting with a system. But I was curious about whether we could simulate an entire social environment—people with memories, relationships, and goals—and let those interactions unfold.

With early foundation models, you could start to imagine describing a person in natural language and having the model generate plausible behavior for them. The exciting question was whether we could move beyond a single response: could an agent remember what happened, use that experience to make plans, and interact with other agents over time? That could give us a new way to prototype social experiences and explore how a community might respond to a change.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the most interesting possibility was using language with foundation models to create richer models of human behavior and generate plausible behavior for people.

sol-6.1.text:
What excited me was the possibility of simulating human behavior. With earlier approaches, you often had to specify a lot of that behavior by hand. Language models suggested a different possibility: could you describe a person—their experiences, their relationships, what matters to them—and have a computational agent behave in a way that reflects that description?

And then, if you put several of those agents together, could meaningful social interactions emerge? That opened up a really interesting space for me, both for building interactive systems and for thinking about how we might study social behavior.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the possibility of simulating human behavior excited him and explains that language models could let agents behave in ways reflecting a person's experiences, relationships, and values.
